name: Hana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven at Fernhill. I do the calf shed first, about sixty calves this time of year, bottles for the young ones, then bedding and checking for scour, which is the runny tummies that can kill a calf. Afternoons I'm usually in the grain store with the old Massey loader, or helping Ivo, the manager, with whatever needs a spare pair of hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up at Fernhill?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a bookkeeper at a builders' merchant in town for twenty-eight years. They were bought by a big chain, the new software did most of what I did, and they offered me redundancy. My cousin worked at Fernhill and said they wanted someone for the calves, so I thought, why not, it's outside and nobody's watching my screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and not like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the calves and the routine. Same jobs, same order, and you can see what you've done at the end of the day. I don't like the cold in February, and I don't like how much I still get wrong. Ivo's patient, but I can see him checking my bedding after I've done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss. Probably over coffee in the farm office. I wouldn't say it online, I don't really do that, and I'm not one for big opinions anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, which suits me fine. I'd do the calves till I'm sixty-six, Lars would keep plumbing, and we'd be all right. I had enough of computers changing my job at the builders' merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep going at Fernhill, keep the savings ticking over, about a hundred and fifty a month. I might ask Ivo if I could learn the telehandler properly, because that's the one machine I'm still scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, maybe. It's like hearing the road outside won't be dug up after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you had enough of computers changing your job. What happened exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over about three years, the new system did the invoices, the stock, the reconciliations, all of it. By the end I was mostly fixing its mistakes and answering the phone. I wasn't angry at anyone. It made sense for the business. It just didn't make sense for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So does it worry you at all, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only small things. Ivo's talked about a feeding system that mixes the calf milk automatically. If that came in, half my mornings would go. But that's a machine, not this AI business, and it's been talked about for two years.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, all that fuss for nothing, over coffee in the farm office. I wouldn't post it anywhere.
S0.think: Nothing changing suits her: calves until 66, Lars plumbing, the two of them all right. She'd had enough of computers changing her job at the builders' merchant.
S0.do: Keeps working at Fernhill and saving about 150 a month. Asks Ivo to teach her the telehandler properly.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like hearing the road won't be dug up after all.
S0.quote: It made sense for the business. It just didn't make sense for me.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's pragmatism is striking: she doesn't blame the merchant that automated her job, she just won't go through it again. Her one worry even here is an automatic calf feeder, which would take half her mornings. She avoids having big opinions in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point. The farm has to keep costs down, and people need work. I'd say that at the coffee table if it came up, but I'd mostly keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Fernhill would be one of the first to change. The family who own it live two hundred miles away and the decisions come from their accountants. If a calf-feeding robot saves them a wage, they'll buy it, and mine's the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and watch what Ivo actually orders, because talk is cheap on farms. I'd put a bit more aside, two hundred a month instead of one fifty, and skip the trip to see my sister this spring. I wouldn't go learning computer things. If they need someone to clean a robot, I can clean a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise in the engine and you hope it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the computer side. What if Ivo asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the minimum to keep my job. I'd learn which buttons to press and nothing else. I did that for the last three years at the merchant, and I can do it again. I'm not going to become a robot person at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lars, at night. He'd say his work's safe because robots can't get under a sink, and I'd say, give them time. And my cousin Birgit, because if they cut at Fernhill, they'd cut us both.

S1.say: I'd say both sides have a point: the farm has to keep costs down and people need work. Mostly I'd keep my head down.
S1.think: She expects Fernhill to change early, because the absent owners' accountants decide, and an automatic calf feeder would replace her wage.
S1.do: Waits to see what Ivo actually orders and raises savings to about 200 a month, skipping a spring trip to her sister. Would learn only the minimum buttons if asked to run a machine.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an engine noise you hope is nothing.
S1.quote: I'm not going to become a robot person at fifty-eight.
S1.fieldNote: Hana's centrism shows as fairness to both sides, even when she expects to lose. Her resistance is quiet and practical: she'd learn the minimum, not refuse outright. The absent owners and their accountants are the closest she comes to blaming anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is happening too fast for anyone, farms included, and the government needs to slow it down or help people through it. I'd say that to anyone, even though I don't usually say much. It's the first time I'd want my vote to count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of work by sixty. Fernhill would have robots before anywhere, and there's nothing else for me. Bookkeeping's gone, the farm's gone, and I'm not going to start something new in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back the minute I heard, everything that isn't food and heat. I'd ask Lars if I could help him on his jobs, carrying and fetching and doing his invoices, because his work might last a bit longer. And I'd look into whether I could take my small pension from the builders' merchant early, even at a loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, adding things up. It's a horrible feeling, not having anything to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helping Lars, is that a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only one I can think of. He's sixty and his back's going, so maybe I'd be useful, holding the torch, writing up the jobs. It's not a career. It's just staying busy and bringing a little in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years of warning, what's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask Ivo straight out what the family's planning. I'd rather know. At the merchant, they told us the week before, and I'd been saving for a holiday. I'd rather know two years out and be miserable than know a week out and be shocked.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for anyone and the government needs to slow it down or help people through it. It's the first time she'd want her vote to count.
S2.think: She'd be out of work by 60, with Fernhill getting robots first and no bookkeeping to go back to, and no will to start something new in two years.
S2.do: Cuts spending to food and heat as soon as she hears and asks Ivo directly what the owners plan. Starts helping Lars on his plumbing jobs and looks into taking her small builders' merchant pension early, even at a loss.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake, with nothing to fall back on.
S2.quote: I'd rather know two years out and be miserable than know a week out and be shocked.
S2.fieldNote: The speed takes away her favourite tactic, waiting and watching. Helping Lars is less a plan than a way to stay busy and bring a little in. Even alarmed, she reaches for politics only in the quietest form: wanting her vote to count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, and I'd want the farm to be honest with us about what's coming. I'd ask at the staff meeting, and I'd keep asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three. If I can stay on at Fernhill until the robots actually come, and keep saving, I might be able to stop with a few lean years before the pension. It's not good, but it's not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving the two hundred a month and put any overtime in too, so by the end we'd have maybe a year's money. I'd make sure the car and the boiler are sorted before it hits, because those are the big bills that sink you. And I'd plan to take the merchant pension at sixty-three, not sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a kind of anxious I know. Like the last years at the merchant. You see it coming and you get your house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money, mainly. A year of savings instead of four months. And Lars would be closer to his own pension too. In the fast one, we're both scrambling. In this one, we're tidying up before we go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be tempted to learn the new machines, with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. More time doesn't make me want to learn it. It makes me want to get out cleanly. I know that sounds stubborn, but I've done one round of that and I'm not doing another.

S3.say: I'd say five years is something, and I'd keep asking at staff meetings for the farm to be honest about what's coming.
S3.think: Five years gets her to 63; staying on until the robots come and saving hard could leave only a few lean years before her pension.
S3.do: Keeps saving about 200 a month plus any overtime, aiming for a year's money, and gets the car and boiler sorted before it hits. Plans to take her merchant pension at 63 instead of 66.
S3.feel: Anxious in a familiar way, like the last years at the merchant when she got her house in order.
S3.quote: In the fast one, we're both scrambling. In this one, we're tidying up before we go.
S3.fieldNote: More warning time doesn't make Hana more willing to learn; it makes her more determined to leave cleanly, which she owns as stubborn. Her focus is the big bills, the car and the boiler, a bookkeeper's instinct. The repeated ask for honesty from the farm is her main demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and nobody can complain they didn't know. I'd probably say that at the coffee table and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be sixty-eight, and I'm planning to stop at sixty-six. The robots can have the calf shed after I've gone, as long as someone tells the calves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Fernhill like normal and keep saving. I'd maybe finally get to see my sister more, without the guilt of spending. I'd tell the twins to think about it, but they're twenty-nine, they'll make their own minds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Like it's somebody else's weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the twins, if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freya's a dental nurse and Nils works in a call centre. I'd tell Nils to get out of that call centre, honestly. I sat next to a phone for twenty-eight years and I know where those jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that wishes you were younger, to see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd be curious what the farm looks like in twenty years, but I don't need to be in it. I left the office because the computer did my job. I'm not chasing it out to the calf shed to learn its new tricks.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and nobody can complain they didn't know, and leave it at that.
S4.think: She's fine: she'd be 68 and plans to stop at 66, so the robots can have the calf shed after she's gone.
S4.do: Carries on at Fernhill as normal, keeps saving and visits her sister more. Tells her son Nils to get out of his call-centre job.
S4.quote: The robots can have the calf shed after I've gone, as long as someone tells the calves.
S4.fieldNote: Hana is calm because the timeline passes her retirement, not because she's at peace with the technology. Her sharpest advice is for her son in a call centre, drawn straight from her own experience. She shows no wish to be part of what comes next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be sixty, with a few months of money and nothing to go back to. What would help is being able to take part of my pension early without losing most of it, and the farm telling us plainly what's coming and when.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the calves. The little ones that you think won't make it and then they're up and butting you a week later. That's the bit I'd be sad to hand over, robot or no robot.

headlineQuote: I left the office because the computer did my job. I'm not chasing it out to the calf shed to learn its new tricks.
portrait: Hana Hansen is 58 and has worked for two years as a junior hand in the calf shed and grain store at Fernhill, a large arable and suckler beef farm run by a manager for a family who live elsewhere. She came to farming after 28 years as a bookkeeper at a builders' merchant, where new software took most of her job, and she has no wish to touch AI tools again. She is practical and middle-of-the-road, sees the farm's point of view as well as her own, and her instinct is to keep her head down and keep costs low. A plateau leaves her calm, steady change makes her uneasy because the estate's accountants decide everything, and AGI in two years alarms her because she'd have no fallback but helping her partner Lars with his plumbing. Ten years of warning lets her see herself retired before it arrives.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be 60, out of work at a farm run by accountants, with a few months of savings and no appetite for learning another new system.
whatWouldHelp: Being allowed to draw part of her pension early without losing most of it, and plain, early warning from the farm about what machines are coming and when.
